title: Carson Block: Building Muddy Waters, Short Selling, Quant Strategies & Market Risk
question: After an activist short seller exposes an alleged corporate fraud, how does management's response typically unfold across the next two quarterly earnings reports?
guest: When it is a fraud, you are backing these people into a corner and their responses are kind of binary. One, they really dig in and keep it up because they think the only way to beat this is to keep doing what they are doing. Or they make a quiet decision to dial stuff down, which often means reducing earnings guidance to take the attention off them. Think about this from an earnings calendar perspective. Say we publish on a company in Q1. They are already doing what they are doing in Q1, so even if they decide to dive below the radar, you are not going to see it in Q1. And if they are still reeling from the shock, they are not going to dial back full-year guidance in Q1 earnings yet, so you will probably get squeezed hard on Q1 earnings. It is Q2 when they start really evaluating how to handle things. If they decide to dial things back, it usually shows up in second-half guidance. But if they decide to outlast you and keep doing it, going into Q2 becomes a binary event where they either true it up or slam the pedal to the floor.

points.core: First-quarter earnings rarely reflect retrenchment because reporting practices are already locked in.
points.note: Accept: company is already mid-quarter, cannot unwind ongoing practices immediately, or is still reeling from initial shock and will not cut full-year guidance in Q1. Do not credit: generic claims that fraud takes time to resolve.

points.core: Unchanged first-quarter results frequently squeeze short sellers as the stock rallies back.
points.note: Accept: stock rebounds against the short on Q1 earnings, causing pain or a squeeze after the initial drop. Do not credit: generic warnings that shorting is risky or stocks can go up.

points.core: Management typically waits until second-quarter forward guidance to quietly dial back aggression.
points.note: Accept: retreat shows up in Q2 via lowered second-half or forward guidance to reduce scrutiny and dive below the radar. Do not credit: vague mention of eventual restatements or SEC action.

points.core: Cornered executives may instead double down in quarter two to outlast shorts.
points.note: Accept: binary Q2 risk where management escalates, ramps aggressive reporting, or fights back to outlast the activist. Do not credit: generic statements that management denies allegations.

There is no fixed script, but a common pattern emerges from well-known cases (Wirecard, Luckin Coffee, Nikola, Adani) and from academic research on short-seller campaigns.

Within days, management usually issues a forceful denial, calling the report misleading and self-interested, and often threatens litigation or asks regulators to investigate the short seller. It may also announce buybacks, insider purchases, or an "independent" review led by the board or an outside firm.

On the first earnings report after the attack, the company typically stays defiant. Management reaffirms guidance, highlights strong headline numbers, offers selective rebuttals, and cites the ongoing review as a reason not to address specifics.

The second report is usually where the paths diverge. If the allegations are weak, the company produces clean audited results and review findings, and the issue fades. If they have substance, cracks appear: delayed filings, auditor resignations or qualified opinions, disclosed regulatory inquiries, executive departures, lowered guidance, or restatements, often framed as unrelated to the short seller's claims.

Research suggests that non-response or vague responses tend to predict worse outcomes than detailed, verifiable rebuttals.

points.why: The candidate describes first-report defiance and reaffirmed guidance without explaining why existing reporting practices or the timing of the exposé delay retrenchment.
The candidate gives no first-quarter stock rebound or resulting short squeeze.
The candidate lists lowered guidance as one possible second-report development without connecting it to a deliberate effort to dial back aggressive reporting and reduce scrutiny.
The candidate makes the second-report outcome depend on the merits of the allegations and omits management's option to escalate aggressive reporting to outlast the short seller.

Management’s response typically shifts from defensive containment in the first post-report quarter to formal accounting and governance reckoning by the second, diverging sharply depending on whether the allegations have merit.

In the first quarterly report, leadership focuses on stabilizing confidence. Empirically, firms facing weak claims often ignore the short seller altogether or pair broad denials with selective supplemental metrics and reaffirmed guidance to project business as usual. However, if external auditors refuse to sign off without independent verification, management frequently delays the quarterly filing, announces a special audit-committee investigation, and limits earnings-call answers by citing the ongoing review.

By the second quarterly report, auditor and legal scrutiny forces substantive resolution. Cleared firms summarize investigation findings, expand risk and internal-control disclosures, and resume normal reporting. Where allegations hold up, initial denials give way to concrete concessions: withdrawn or reset guidance, material-weakness disclosures, asset write-downs or restatements, regulatory subpoena disclosures, and executive or auditor turnover.

points.why: The response attributes reaffirmed guidance to projecting confidence when claims are weak and gives no reason ongoing reporting practices would delay retrenchment.
The response does not connect first-quarter earnings to a stock rebound that squeezes short sellers.
The response frames second-quarter guidance changes as concessions forced by auditor and legal scrutiny and omits the deliberate choice to lower forward guidance to draw less attention.
The response does not describe management escalating aggressive reporting in the second quarter to outlast the short seller.

In the first quarterly report following a short-seller attack, management typically mounts an aggressive defense, dismissing the allegations as distorted and attacking the short seller’s financial motives. During this initial earnings cycle, executives emphasize business-as-usual momentum, lean on adjusted metrics, and sometimes announce share buybacks or insider purchases to project confidence. Simultaneously, the board often commissions an independent or audit committee review, which management cites on the earnings call to deflect pointed analyst questions while promising fuller answers once the inquiry concludes.

By the second quarterly report, heightened scrutiny from auditors, regulators, and commercial partners forces a divergence between vindication and escalating crisis. When allegations lack merit, management uses this second report to close the chapter, releasing clean investigation findings, expanding disclosures around contested accounting areas, and highlighting resilient cash flows. When underlying improprieties exist, however, the defensive facade usually fractures in the second quarter: external auditors demand expanded testing that triggers delayed filings, key performance definitions quietly shift, guidance is cut under the guise of external headwinds or "short-seller distraction," and disclosures of regulatory subpoenas, restatements, or executive departures frequently follow.

There isn't a fixed script, but research and well-known cases show a common pattern. Brendel and Ryans (2021) found that roughly half of targeted firms respond publicly, usually within days.

**First earnings report:** Management usually goes on the offense. They call the short report misleading or self-interested and stress "strong fundamentals." They often add disclosure on the disputed items, such as revenue recognition, related parties or cash balances. They may announce buybacks, insider purchases, an independent board review or outside counsel, and sometimes threaten to sue. Guidance is usually kept the same so things look normal.

**Second earnings report:** This is where outcomes split. When the allegations are weak, the firm often reports clean results, the review finds nothing material, and the stock partly recovers. When they have substance, problems tend to show up here. Common signs are a delayed 10-Q, an auditor resigning or raising concerns, an SEC or DOJ inquiry being disclosed, write-downs, guidance cuts, or executives departing. That pattern played out at Wirecard and Luckin Coffee. Studies such as Ljungqvist and Qian (2016) find that targeted firms often keep underperforming afterward, which suggests the early denials are frequently not borne out.

In the first quarterly earnings report after an activist short seller alleges fraud, management rarely admits wrongdoing outright. Executives typically adopt a defensive posture, either dismissing the claims as biased and inaccurate through rebuttals or announcing an independent audit committee review while emphasizing core fundamentals. On the earnings call, leadership often leans on scripted legal disclaimers, limits Q&A about the allegations, and pairs reassurances with supplemental disclosures or share buybacks to steady the stock. If the claims raise serious accounting red flags, auditors may decline to sign off, forcing the company to delay its filing.

By the second quarterly report, the response usually diverges based on whether the allegations hold up. If internal reviews find no material issues, management declares the matter closed and refocuses investors on operations and guidance. If the allegations have merit, the tone shifts from denial to damage control, with filings disclosing material control weaknesses, restatements, regulatory inquiries, executive or auditor departures, withdrawn guidance, and rising legal costs.

Efforts to steady the stock do not establish a rebound on unchanged first-quarter earnings that squeezes short sellers.
The response frames withdrawn guidance as damage control when allegations have merit and omits the quiet use of lower second-quarter forward guidance to reduce scrutiny.

noweb.answer:
In the first quarterly earnings report following an activist short seller's fraud allegations, management typically mounts a forceful defense. Executives dismiss the report as inaccurate or self-interested, emphasize core operational metrics to reassure investors, and often announce an internal or board-led investigation, occasionally paired with a share buyback to signal confidence. During the earnings call, leadership tends to deflect granular analyst questions by citing the ongoing review while trying to maintain existing financial guidance.

By the second quarterly report, the response generally shifts from public pushback to concrete consequences or normalization. If the allegations uncover real issues, this quarter often brings delayed filings, accounting restatements, asset write-downs, lowered guidance, leadership or auditor turnover, and disclosures of regulatory inquiries such as SEC subpoenas. If the internal review finds no wrongdoing, management instead pivots toward rebuilding credibility through expanded financial disclosures, tighter governance controls, and a renewed focus on routine operating performance.

There’s no standard two-quarter sequence. In a study of 351 activist short-seller reports, only 31% drew a public response from the targeted company. There’s no reliable two-quarter script. Management often responds immediately with a denial or rebuttal. At the first earnings report, executives may repeat that defense, answer analysts’ questions, and say whether the board has opened an independent review.

By the second report, investors generally expect evidence that tests the original response. If the review supports management, executives may publish its findings and explain how the disputed figures reconcile with the accounts. If it uncovers problems, the company may revise guidance, announce a restatement, or disclose leadership changes. A review can also remain open beyond the second quarter. The most informative comparison is what management claimed in the first report and what it can substantiate in the second.
